name: Reporting the Total Hours Each Employee Worked (Case 1)
description:
Suppose we have an input file that contains information about how many hours each employee of a company has worked. The file looks like the following (Employee's name, Hours):
Erica 7.5 8.5 10.25 8 8.5
Erin 10.5 11.5 12 11 10.75
Simone 8 8 8
...
Construct a program that reads this file and calculates the total number of hours worked by each individual. Make sure that the program handles each specific exception that could occur.

comments.content: We need to read the file name that the user enters. To read the input string from the user, we need to define a Scanner object.

We can create a Scanner object using the operator new, as shown in this statement. The System.in object represents the standard input stream, which by default is the keyboard. It tells the java compiler that the input will be provided through keyboard.
We prompt the user to enter the name of the file.
We need to read the file name that the user enters and store it in a variable. We read the string by calling the next() method.
This statement creates a JWorkHours1 object using the new keyword and empty parentheses. The variable jwh holds a reference to a JWorkHours1 object.
This statement invokes the method reportWorkHours of the jwh and passes the file name received from the user as its argument.

We need to declare the method that processes the employees file specified as the method's parameter. We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as void, as it does not return any value.
The try blocks tries to execute the code within it. The statements in the try block may throw several types of exception.
If an error is encountered, the try block code execution is stopped and transferred down to the catch block(s).

We want to read a text file; therefore, we need to use a FileReader and wrap it in a BufferedReader. This statement create a FileReader object using the new keyword and empty parentheses. The variable fr holds a reference to a FileReader object.
We wrap a BufferedReader around the FileReader because the BufferedReader buffers the input to make the reading process much faster. The variable br holds a reference to a BufferedReader object.
We define a string variable to hold the content of each line that the BufferedReader object reads from the file. We set it to null.

We need to read the lines as long as we have not reached the end of the file. Therefore, we need to use a loop structure. Since we don't know ahead of time how many times the loop will be repeated, we need to use a while loop. The condition in the while loop tests whether the body of the loop should be repeated, so it should test whether the line that is read is not null.

We could read a line by invoking the readLine method of the BufferedReader object. Here, we compare the result of calling the readLine method to null. We assign the result of calling the readLine method to variable line because we need to process it in the body of the while loop.
The body of the while loop is repeated as long as the line that is read is not null. The loop terminates when the loop condition evaluates to false, that is when the line that is read is null.
We need to split the line into words and store the words in an array.
We use split() method with ' ' as its argument because we want the split method to separate strings using a single space character.
tokens[0] gives us the element at index 0 of the array that represents the employee's name.
We need variable total to maintain a running total, which means the sum of the hours the employee worked. Of course, the total should be initialized with 0.

We use a for loop to iterate over the hours reported for the employee. We can get the hours that the employee has worked by accessing the second through the last element in the array of line tokens. We need the indexes to start at 1 with every integer number up to but not including the array length.

Note that the loop starts at 1 because the value at the index 0 of the array is the employee's name. The hours the employee has worked start from the second element in the array of line tokens. Also, note that the function tokens.length returns the number of the values in the array of line tokens.

In the first part of the loop header, we define a control variable i and initialize it to 1. In the second part of the loop header, we test whether the control variable has reached the termination threshold. The loop is repeated if the control variable is less than tokens.length (array length) and terminates when the control variable reaches tokens.length. In the third part of the loop header, we increment the control variable by 1 after each iteration of the loop.
Note that the first part is executed once before the loop starts, the second part is executed before each iteration, and the third part is executed after each iteration of the loop.
Also, note that the increment operator (++) adds 1 to the value of variable i and the result is stored back into the variable i. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement i = i + 1.
If an error is encountered during calculating the total hours the employee has worked, the try block code execution is stopped and transferred down to the catch block.

We need to add each reported hour to the running total that is stored in variable total. So, in each iteration, we add the reported hour to the variable total and store the result into the variable total.
We get the reported hour by accessing the element at index i of the array of line tokens. We need to covert this value to a floating-point number by calling the Double.parseDouble method.

Note that we could perform the conversion to a double and addition in the same line. Also, note that each value that is stored in the array of line tokens is a string. Therefore, we need to convert the hours employee has worked into a number. We convert each hour to a floating-point number by calling the Double.parseDouble() method because the reported hours could have a decimal point.

The += operator adds the reported hour to the value of the variable total and the result is stored in the variable total. Thus, this statement is equivalent to the statement total = total + Double.parseDouble(tokens[i]).

We need to handle the NumberFormatException. This error occurs when an hour that is reported for the employee is not a number and we call the method Double.parseDouble() to convert that value to a double.
The body of this catch block gets executed only if a reported hour in the line is not a number. Otherwise, the body of this catch statement is skipped.
This statement prints to the default standard output stream the error that caused the NumberFormatException. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

This statement concatenates the content of the given strings, variable name and total to print the total hours each employee has worked. We concatenate the content of these variables using the + operator.
Note that the concatenating and printing are done in the same line. That is, we don't have to store the concatenated string to a new variable at first and then print it in the next line.
Note that the + operator creates a new string from the contents of its operands joined. This string will be printed by the print method and followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

We're done reading the file; so, we need to close the BufferedReader object. Closing a BufferedReader object will also close the Reader object from which the BufferedReader is reading. Therefore, we don't need to close the FileReader object (i.e., object referred by variable fr) when the BufferedReader object is closed .
We need to handle the FileNotFoundException. This error occurs when the file could not be found.
The body of this catch block gets executed only if the file could not be found. Otherwise, the body of this catch statement is skipped.
This statement prints to the default standard output stream the error that caused the FileNotFoundException. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
We need to handle the IOException. This error occurs when an error occurs when trying to read/close the file.
The body of this catch block gets executed only if an error occurs when trying to read/close the file. Otherwise, the body of this catch statement is skipped.
This statement prints to the default standard output stream the error that caused the IOException. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
